purpose: Obscure and enterprise inference accelerators with unusually strong memory capacity, bandwidth, or power characteristics. Vendor TOPS/TFLOPS and benchmark claims are retained with provenance and are not normalized across architectures.

hardware.quantization_compatibility: Hardware exposes BF16, FP8, INT8 and INT4. Furiosa publishes precompiled model bundles and per-model quantization recipes; this is not a drop-in GGUF/CUDA accelerator and models generally use the Furiosa compilation/runtime path.

llm_suitability.practical_guidance: 48GB HBM3 and 1.5TB/s are exceptionally strong for supported 8B-32B dense models and multi-card larger-model serving. Furiosa documents Llama 3.3 70B FP8 on four cards, so single-card 70B deployment should not be inferred from capacity alone.
llm_suitability.vendor_software_evidence: Furiosa's 2026 supported-model matrix validates multiple Llama, Qwen, EXAONE and GPT-OSS architectures; performance tuning status varies by model.

hardware.efficiency_notes: At the current 180W product specification, raw memory bandwidth is approximately 8.33GB/s/W, unusually high for a 48GB accelerator. This is a hardware bandwidth metric, not tokens/joule.

pricing.note: Furiosa states RNGD is in mass production and available as a standalone PCIe card, but no defensible public numeric card price was found.

source_caveats: Older Furiosa developer pages have shown 150W TDP, while current public product/spec pages and the April 2026 mass-production announcement specify 180W. This record uses the current 180W product value and preserves the discrepancy as provenance.

hardware.quantization_compatibility: Qualcomm documents FP16 and integer inference paths and optimized generative-AI model conversion. Do not assume GGUF/AWQ/GPTQ files run directly; deployment uses Qualcomm's compiler/runtime and precompiled/optimized model ecosystem.

llm_suitability.vendor_model_capacity: up to 120B parameters in current on-prem appliance positioning
llm_suitability.vendor_performance_claim: up to 300 tokens/s on Llama 3.1 8B in Qualcomm's on-prem appliance material
llm_suitability.practical_guidance: 128GB accelerator memory is unusually large at 150W and can avoid sharding for many large optimized models, but software portability is materially narrower than CUDA/ROCm/MLX.

hardware.efficiency_notes: 128GB at 150W is approximately 1.17W/GB of accelerator memory. The 3.65GB/s/W bandwidth ratio is lower than HBM accelerators but capacity-per-watt is unusually strong.

pricing.note: Qualcomm exposes contact-sales and OEM on-prem appliance channels; no defensible public standalone-card retail price was verified.

hardware.architecture: MemryX MX3 compute-at-memory/dataflow, four MX3 ICs
hardware.external_dram: none; model weights/operators are stored on-chip within supported capacity
hardware.host_interface: PCIe Gen3 via M.2 2280 M-key; module exposes two 2-lane PCIe links
hardware.quantization_compatibility: The module stores up to about 80M 4-bit or 40M 8-bit weight parameters. MemryX states models can often be deployed without user-driven quantization/retraining, but transformer support remains limited and compiler-dependent. This is not a general GGUF LLM accelerator.

llm_suitability.practical_guidance: Parameter storage limits are orders of magnitude below modern 1B+ LLM weight sets. SDK 2.2 supports Attention, MultiHeadAttention and GroupedQueryAttention, but MemryX explicitly says transformer support is still limited. Best treated as a low-power CV/hybrid-transformer accelerator rather than a local-chat LLM device.

hardware.efficiency_notes: Typical module power is about 8W and average maximum 10W. This makes it highly attractive for always-on vision or small transformer subgraphs, but its limited on-chip weight capacity prevents direct comparison with DRAM/HBM LLM accelerators.

pricing.note: Qty-1 price. Mouser showed zero stock, 64 units on order, expected 2026-08-28 when checked.
